args.subject: User Tax Query
args.body: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?

User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Thanks — good, clear info. I sent a note to my tax-helper service and will help you here with the tax-treatment, a quick estimate, and exactly which forms to expect. I have a few clarifying questions below so I can give precise numbers; meanwhile here’s a clear summary of how to treat each item and what to expect.

Quick summary (high-level)
- Your W-2 wages ($68,200) and the bank/investment interest/dividends are taxable on Form 1040.
- The $16,300 fro

m photography is self-employment income and should be reported on Schedule C; business expenses reduce that amount.
- You’ll owe self-employment tax on your net photography profit (Schedule SE); half of that SE tax is an above-the-line deduction on Schedule 1.
- Home-office deduction is available for the self-employment activity. Using the regular method (pro rata share of rent) gives a much bigger deduction here than the simplified method.
- Student loan interest deduction: the maximum annual deduction is

limited (up to $2,500) and phases out above certain MAGI levels — your income is near the phaseout range, so you may be partially or fully limited. I need a clarification below to determine this exactly.
- Charitable gift ($1,500) is an itemized deduction — but unless you have additional itemizable items, you’ll very likely take the standard deduction (single) for 2024.
- Because you live in Texas, there’s typically no state income tax return.

Detailed treatment and calculations

1) Self-employment income

(photography: $16,300)
- Report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business).
- Deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses on Schedule C (camera gear, supplies, advertising, business portion of phone, mileage, etc.). If the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” are photography business expenses, they belong on Schedule C (not as employee unreimbursed expenses).
- Self-employment tax: compute net profit × 92.35% × 15.3% (Schedule SE). Example quick estimate (if no business expenses):
  - Net = $16,300 → taxabl

e amount for SE = 16,300 × 0.9235 ≈ $15,053 → SE tax ≈ $15,053 × 0.153 ≈ $2,303.
  - Half the SE tax (~$1,151) is an adjustment on Schedule 1 and reduces your AGI.
- Note: If you actually have business expenses (e.g., that $1,050), plug those in and the SE tax and AGI will be lower.

2) Home office (120 sq ft exclusive; total 740 sq ft; rent $1,750/mo)
- Two methods: regular (actual-expense) or simplified ($5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft).
  - Regular method: business-use percentage = 120 / 740 ≈ 16.216% → annual

rent = $1,750 × 12 = $21,000 → deductible share = 21,000 × 0.16216 ≈ $3,405. (You can also prorate utilities and renter’s insurance if you pay them.)
  - Simplified method: 120 sq ft × $5 = $600.
- The regular method yields ~ $3,405 vs $600 with the simplified method — so the regular method is clearly better here.
- For the regular method you generally complete Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and attach it to Schedule C.
- Important: the home office must be used regularly and exclusively

for business (you said exclusive — that qualifies).

3) Bank/investment income ($2,100 Capital One 360; $420 Merrill Edge)
- These are typically interest (1099‑INT) and/or dividends (1099‑DIV). They are taxable on Form 1040.
- If total taxable interest + ordinary dividends > $1,500, you must file Schedule B (interest and ordinary dividends). Your totals ($2,520) exceed $1,500 → use Schedule B.
- If you had securities sales, capital gains/losses are reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D (noted here in case Me

rrill Edge included sales).

4) Student loan interest ($5,100 listed)
- The student loan interest deduction (an above-the-line adjustment on Schedule 1) has a maximum annual deduction (generally up to $2,500 per year) and phases out when your MAGI is above a certain level.
- You cannot deduct interest paid in prior years on this year’s return — the deduction applies to interest you actually paid during the tax year. Clarify whether the $5,100 is interest you paid in 2024 or a multi-year total (see questions

below).
- Given your income range, you may be partially or fully phased out — I’ll compute exact phaseout once we confirm your MAGI/adjustments.

5) Charitable contribution ($1,500 to Salvation Army)
- Charitable contributions are deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A).
- Compare total itemized deductions vs. the standard deduction for single filers for 2024; with a single $1,500 gift, you are very likely better off taking the standard deduction unless you have other sizable itemizable deductions (med

ical, state/local taxes, mortgage interest, etc.).

6) Unreimbursed expenses ($1,050)
- Are these related to the photography business? If yes → Schedule C business expenses.
- If they are unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job, they are not deductible for federal returns under current law (TCJA suspended miscellaneous itemized deductions through 2025).

7) Estimated tax / withholding
- Because you have self-employment income, you’ll owe both income tax and self-employment tax. If your employer with

holding doesn’t cover your total tax liability, you should make quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040-ES) to avoid underpayment penalties.

Which forms you will most likely need
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return).
- Schedule 1 (additional income and adjustments) — for adjustments like student loan interest and the deduction for half of SE tax.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — for photography income and expenses.
- Schedule SE (Self-Employment Tax) — to calculate SE tax.
- For

m 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you choose the regular home-office method.
- Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends) — because your interest total exceeds $1,500.
- Schedule A (Itemized Deductions) — only if you itemize (I expect you’ll probably take the standard deduction).
- Form 8949 / Schedule D — only if you had securities sales reported by Merrill Edge.
- 1099s & W-2: have your W-2 (Coastal Manufacturing), any 1099-NEC/1099-MISC/1099-K for photography (if received), 1099-INT

(bank interest), 1099-DIV or 1099-B from Merrill Edge as applicable.

Actionable recommendations
- Use the regular home-office method (Form 8829) — it gives a much larger deduction for your situation.
- Put business-related unreimbursed expenses on Schedule C (if they relate to photography).
- Calculate student loan interest deduction carefully — likely capped at $2,500 and may phase out; confirm the $5,100 is 2024 interest.
- Likely take the standard deduction unless you have other itemizable items (mortga

ge interest, large medical expenses, big state/local taxes).
- Keep receipts, mileage logs, rent and utility receipts, donation receipts, and 1099s/1098/1099-INT/1099-DIV paperwork.

Questions I need to finalize exact numbers
1. Is the $5,100 of student loan interest interest you paid in 2024 (tax year 2024)? Or is that an aggregate from prior years (2018–2021)? Only interest actually paid in 2024 can be deducted on your 2024 return.
2. Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for the photog

raphy (i.e., incurred for the self-employment activity) or unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job?
3. Do you have any other deductible expenses (mortgage interest, state/local taxes, big medical expenses, more charitable gifts, etc.)?
4. Were the $2,100 and $420 interest payments reported to you on 1099‑INT / 1099‑DIV? Any 1099‑NEC or 1099‑K from photography clients?
5. Do you want me to run an approximate tax liability estimate (federal only) including estimated self-employment tax and show whethe

r you owe estimated taxes or will get a refund? If so, I can produce a draft calculation given the answers to the questions above.

If you want, I can:
- Run a worked example (approximate AGI, taxable income, and estimated federal tax + SE tax) using reasonable assumptions.
- Draft a checklist/worksheet of all receipts and figures you should gather to prepare your return or to hand to a tax preparer.

Tell me the answers to the clarifying questions (especially #1 and #2) and I’ll run the specific calculatio
n and say whether you should itemize and exactly how much you could deduct for the home office and student loan interest.
